subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Note for Aditi's parents, from her violin teacher. Aditi arrived early and played the opening piece from last term, the one she has known by heart since March. She played it three times, smiling each time, and asked if she could play it again. When I turned to the new page with the fast finger shifts, she said her hand was tired. So I asked her to play only the four hard bars, slowly, five times, and we marked each try with a pencil tick. By the fifth try the notes were cleaner. She frowned but stayed. Please let her start home practice with those four bars. Damini, music teacher

qa.q: How many times did Aditi play the old piece when she arrived?
qa.a: She played it three times, smiling each time.

qa.q: What might Aditi be feeling when she says her hand is tired at the new page?
qa.a: She is probably uneasy or discouraged. The old piece feels good and the new page is hard, so a tired hand may be a way to avoid the difficult part.

qa.q: What small step could Aditi's parents take to help at home?
qa.a: They could ask her to play the four hard bars slowly at the start of practice, before the piece she already knows.

qa.q: How does Damini see Aditi's repeated playing of the old piece?
qa.a: Damini sees it as enjoyable but not much practice, which is why the teacher moved her to the hard bars and marked each try.

grounding: Shows a child repeating a mastered violin piece because it feels good while the difficult bars are where growth lives.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Tuesday evening. Played my favourite keyboard tune again, the rain song. Six times! It feels so nice when my fingers already know where to go. Deepika didi came in and listened and said it sounded lovely, then asked why I never play the second page. I said it's boring and I get it wrong. She said the wrong bit is where fingers learn. She showed me just two bars, left hand only, very slowly. I got them wrong seven times and I was cross. Then once right. Tomorrow I will do the two bars before the rain song, not after. Leela

qa.q: How many times did Leela play the rain song?
qa.a: Leela played the rain song six times.

qa.q: Why was Leela cross while practising the two bars?
qa.a: Leela felt frustrated because getting the two bars wrong seven times felt worse than the easy tune that always goes right. 😕

qa.q: What choice did Leela make for the next day's practice?
qa.a: Leela decided to play the two bars before the rain song instead of after, so the hard part comes first.

qa.q: How does Deepika see the wrong notes Leela plays?
qa.a: Deepika treats the wrong notes as the place where fingers learn, so the second page is worth the effort.

grounding: Shows a child replaying an already easy tune for pleasure and only later working on the hard bars.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Monday, Kalyani wrote "3 hours" in her practice log. The guitar lay across her knees but her eyes kept going to the phone, and the change from G to C still buzzed every single time. Thursday, her friend Mehak, who plays in the school band, listened for two minutes and asked, "Which part keeps failing?" Kalyani said the G to C change, and realised she had never once stopped on it. Mehak told her to set a timer and repeat only that change. The following Tuesday the log read "25 minutes, phone in the other room". She played G to C ten times, stopped when her ring finger lagged, fixed the angle, and the chord rang clean.

qa.q: What did Kalyani write in her practice log on Monday?
qa.a: She wrote "3 hours" in her practice log.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling on Thursday when she realised she had never stopped on the G to C change?
qa.a: She was probably a little embarrassed and surprised, since three hours had gone by without her ever working on the exact spot that failed.

qa.q: What turning point led to the clean chord on Tuesday?
qa.a: She moved the phone away, isolated the G to C change, repeated it with a timer and stopped to fix what made her ring finger lag.

qa.q: What did Mehak notice that Kalyani had missed?
qa.a: Mehak, who plays in the band, noticed that one specific change kept failing and asked her which part it was, which turned long hours into targeted work.

grounding: Shows a teenager logging long half-attending hours with no gain, then improving through a focused fix of one weakness.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Beta, I am Gargi, and I will tell you about my sitar years. At fifteen I sat for four hours every day and wrote the hours in a notebook like a shopkeeper. My teacher, Uday Sir, only nodded. After a whole season I was no better, and I did not understand why. One evening Uday Sir said, "Play only bar twelve, with the clock ticking." Each time I rushed, he stopped me at once and made me start again. Twenty minutes, then he sent me home. I was furious. By Saturday bar twelve was clean, and that was more than four hours a day had done in months.

qa.q: How many hours a day did Gargi sit with the sitar at fifteen?
qa.a: Gargi sat for four hours every day.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when Uday Sir stopped the playing again and again on bar twelve?
qa.a: Gargi was furious, because being stopped every time the playing rushed felt like a punishment, though the task was only one bar.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Gargi's progress?
qa.a: Playing only bar twelve with a ticking clock and being corrected at once whenever she rushed, instead of sitting for long hours.

qa.q: Why might Uday Sir have stopped Gargi so quickly each time the tempo rushed?
qa.a: Uday Sir could see the exact weak spot, and correcting it at the moment it happened let Gargi fix it before it became a habit.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling logging many hours with no improvement until concentrated work with immediate correction on one weak bar.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Chaitanya, the harmonium teacher at the village school, watched Preeti's hands fly through a film song at the Friday class. The runs were bright but smudged, and he knew why: she had stopped doing her scales weeks ago. "Come, play sa re ga ma with me first," he said. She sighed. "That is boring, sir." He smiled. "The fast run in your song is only this scale wearing a costume. If the plain scale is muddy, the costume will be muddy too." They played it slowly together, twice. Preeti heard the smudge on the fourth note and stopped by herself. "Again," she said quietly.

qa.q: Who was watching Preeti play at the Friday class?
qa.a: Chaitanya, the harmonium teacher at the village school, was watching Preeti.

qa.q: What might Chaitanya be worried about as he listens to the smudged runs?
qa.a: He is worried that the gaps left by skipped scales will show later and hold Preeti back, though he handles it gently instead of scolding.

qa.q: What could Chaitanya try if Preeti still finds scales boring?
qa.a: He could connect each scale to a bar of her favourite song so she can hear how the basic notes make the fun part clean.

qa.q: What is it like for Preeti when Chaitanya asks her to play the plain scale?
qa.a: Preeti finds it dull at first and sighs, but once she hears the smudge herself she wants to try again, which shows the request moved from a chore to something she cares about.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a student skip fundamentals for a flashy song and gently explaining how basics make the song possible.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Coach Leila stood by the fence at the community pitch while the under-fifteens ran passing drills against the wall. Siddiq had wandered to the corner with a ball, practising step-overs. His flicks were quick and his first touch was loose, and Leila had seen it twice already this week. She jogged over. "Show me the step-over." He did it three times. "Now pass to me with your weaker foot." The ball rolled away. Siddiq laughed, embarrassed. "Those step-overs only work if the ball sticks to your foot afterwards," Leila said. "Give me ten passes, then you can show off." He grinned and went back to the wall.

qa.q: Where was Siddiq practising step-overs?
qa.a: Siddiq was practising step-overs in the corner of the pitch with a ball.

qa.q: What might Leila be feeling as Leila sees the loose first touch behind the flicks?
qa.a: Leila is probably concerned that the missing basics will show later, yet patient and wanting Siddiq to keep enjoying the game, which is why the request stays friendly.

qa.q: How could Leila keep the standard without making Siddiq lose interest?
qa.a: She can let him keep his step-overs as a reward after the passing drills, and explain that the tricks only work if his touch is secure.

qa.q: What would change for Siddiq if Leila had simply told him to stop showing off?
qa.a: He might have felt scolded and shut down, whereas being asked to show the trick first and then link it to control helps him see why the drills matter.

grounding: Shows a coach noticing a boy skipping basic drills for flashy tricks and holding the standard gently by explaining how basics enable them.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
subtype: Working at the edge of ability [Actor]
passage: Siddiq chalked his hands and looked at the orange route on the gym wall. It was one grade harder than anything he had finished. Tariq, holding the rope below, called, "You sure?" "Not sure at all," Siddiq said, and started up. At the third hold from the top his fingers slipped and he dropped, swinging in the harness. Second try, the same spot. Third try, he stopped to study the wall from the floor and saw a foothold he had ignored. On the fourth attempt he stretched, hung, wobbled and clipped the last bolt with shaking arms. His forearms burned. He was grinning anyway.

qa.q: How many attempts did Siddiq make before he clipped the last bolt?
qa.a: He made four attempts before he clipped the last bolt.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when he said he was not sure at all and started up anyway?
qa.a: He was nervous but determined, willing to risk falling because the route sat just beyond what he could do.

qa.q: What did Siddiq do differently on the third try that helped him?
qa.a: He stopped to study the wall from the floor, spotted a foothold he had ignored and used it on the next attempt.

qa.q: What is it like for Tariq to hold the rope while Siddiq keeps falling?
qa.a: Tariq has to trust the grip and stay steady while Siddiq fails, and his "You sure?" shows care rather than doubt.

grounding: Shows a learner choosing a route just above current skill, failing repeatedly and getting through by adjusting.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
subtype: Working at the edge of ability [Actor]
passage: In the carpentry workshop at the polytechnic, Chetan pinned a sheet of drawings above his bench: a dovetail joint, a difficult one for a first-year. Nirmala, the instructor, passed and raised an eyebrow. "That is above where you are." "That is why I picked it," Chetan said. The first joint gapped. The second split at the corner. He swept the offcuts into the bin and marked the saw line again, thinner this time. By closing time the fifth joint fit with a hairline gap. He held it to the light. Nirmala looked, tapped it with a knuckle and said, "Do the sixth tomorrow, and bring the failed ones too."

qa.q: What joint did Chetan pin above his bench?
qa.a: Chetan pinned a drawing of a dovetail joint above his bench.

qa.q: Why did Chetan pick a joint above his level, and what does that show about how he sees mistakes?
qa.a: Chetan wanted a real stretch and treats gaps and splits as the cost of learning, so he is willing to feel the discomfort of not managing it yet.

qa.q: What did Chetan change after the second joint split?
qa.a: He marked the saw line again, thinner this time, and kept trying until the fifth joint fit with a hairline gap.

qa.q: Why might Nirmala ask Chetan to bring the failed joints too?
qa.a: Nirmala can see how the failures show where the technique needs work, and keeping them lets Chetan learn from each error.

grounding: Shows a committed student choosing a task just beyond current skill and accepting repeated failure as the price of growth.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Vidya had a placement interview in three weeks, and every evening she gave herself one narrow target. Tonight it was "stop saying basically". She propped her phone on the shelf, talked for two minutes about her final-year project and played the recording back while her flatmate Naveen washed dishes. Nine "basically"s. She wrote the number on a sticky note and stuck it on the wall. Second recording, with a slow breath before each sentence: three. Naveen looked up. "That one sounded like you." Vidya circled the three, added the date, and wrote tomorrow's target under it: "finish sentences without trailing off".

qa.q: How many times did Vidya say "basically" in the first recording?
qa.a: She said "basically" nine times in the first recording.

qa.q: What might Vidya be feeling when she hears the second recording?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and encouraged, since her count fell from nine to three and it sounded like her own voice.

qa.q: Why does Vidya write the count on a note and set a new target for tomorrow?
qa.a: The written number gives honest feedback and the narrow target lets her fix one thing at a time instead of vaguely practising.

qa.q: How does Naveen's comment help Vidya?
qa.a: Naveen, who has been listening, gives an outside opinion that the second recording sounded like her, which backs up the count she measured herself.

grounding: Shows a learner setting one narrow target per session, reviewing a recording and fixing one thing at a time.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage:
"What's the target today?" Deepika asked, rolling the ball across the court.
"Elbow under the ball. Just that."
"How many shots?"
"Twenty. I'll tick each one that goes in."
"And how will you know if your elbow really was under it?"
Maria held up her phone. "You film me from the side."
They did the twenty. Afterwards they watched the clip together, pausing on shot eleven. "There. Elbow's out again when you're tired," Deepika said. Maria wrote 11 in the notebook: "elbow drifts late". "Tomorrow, same target, but ten shots, rest, ten shots." Deepika nodded. "Good. Keep it that narrow."

qa.q: How many shots did Maria plan to take?
qa.a: Maria planned to take twenty shots and tick each one that went in.

qa.q: What does Maria want to know about her elbow when she asks Deepika to film from the side?
qa.a: Maria wants honest evidence of whether her elbow really stays under the ball, because she does not trust how it feels.

qa.q: What did Maria change in her plan after watching the clip?
qa.a: She noted that her elbow drifts late and planned ten shots, a rest and ten more shots the next day with the same target.

qa.q: Why might Deepika keep the target to one thing?
qa.a: Deepika sees that fixing a single thing at once makes the feedback clear, so Maria can tell what caused any change.

grounding: Shows a learner with a narrow target per session who reviews recorded feedback and fixes one thing at a time.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Saurabh had thrown pots at the wheel behind his uncle's shop in the kasba for seven weeks, and they still looked the same: lopsided, thick at the base. He said to his neighbour Gurpreet, "I think I should try painting instead." Gurpreet kept stacking firewood and didn't answer straight away. "Show me the first bowl you made," he said. Saurabh dug it out of the shelf. Next to it he set the bowl from that morning. The walls were thinner, the rim rounder. He stood there holding both, not sure what he was looking at. "Huh," he said, and went back to the wheel.

qa.q: How long had Saurabh been throwing pots at the wheel?
qa.a: Saurabh had thrown pots at the wheel for seven weeks.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he told Gurpreet he might try painting?
qa.a: He was discouraged and tempted to quit, because seven weeks of effort still seemed to produce the same lopsided pots.

qa.q: What made Saurabh change his mind about switching hobbies?
qa.a: Setting his first bowl beside the morning's bowl showed thinner walls and a rounder rim, which was progress he had not noticed.

qa.q: Why might Gurpreet ask for the first bowl instead of giving advice?
qa.a: Gurpreet may want Saurabh to see the change for himself, since progress that builds unseen is easier to believe than someone else's reassurance.

grounding: Shows a practitioner with no visible progress for weeks, tempted to switch hobbies, until a comparison shows skill consolidating.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Layla's sketchbook had a watercolour every morning for six weeks, and by week five she hated all of them. Over coffee in the studio café in Lisbon, she told Rosa, "I'm getting nowhere. Maybe I should switch to ceramics." Rosa turned the pages back to the first week and laid the book flat. The early washes were streaky and flat. The recent ones held soft edges and a clear light. Layla stared. "I didn't see it happening." Rosa shrugged. "You were too close." Layla closed the book slowly. That night she set a fresh page and mixed the blue again.

qa.q: How often had Layla painted a watercolour in her sketchbook?
qa.a: Layla painted a watercolour every morning for six weeks.

qa.q: What was Layla feeling by week five, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Layla felt frustrated and stuck, and she says she is getting nowhere and might switch to ceramics.

qa.q: What did Layla do after Rosa turned the pages back to week one?
qa.a: Layla closed the book slowly, then that night set a fresh page and mixed the blue again, choosing to continue instead of switching to ceramics.

qa.q: How might Rosa see Layla's progress differently from Layla?
qa.a: Rosa looks at the pages from a distance and sees streaky early washes next to soft edges and clear light, while Layla was too close to notice the change.

grounding: Shows an artist who sees no progress for weeks and is tempted to quit, until earlier pages reveal quiet consolidation.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage: Akash sir said the legs of my cow were too short. I had worked on that cow all morning. My face went hot and I said, "Then the whole drawing is bad." I put my head on the desk. He did not get cross. He said, "I did not say the drawing is bad. I said the legs are short." Then he gave me an eraser and asked me to measure the legs against the body with my pencil. I did not want to, but I did it. The legs got longer. The cow stood up better. I still felt a little bit sad. Sarita

qa.q: What did Akash sir say was wrong with the cow?
qa.a: Akash sir said the legs of the cow were too short.

qa.q: Why did Sarita say the whole drawing was bad?
qa.a: Sarita felt hurt and ashamed, as if the correction about the legs meant the whole cow and the morning's work were judged.

qa.q: What helped Sarita move from putting the head down to fixing the drawing?
qa.a: Akash sir stayed calm, said only the legs were short, and gave an eraser and a way to measure the legs against the body.

qa.q: How does Akash sir see the short legs?
qa.a: Akash sir sees them as one part of the drawing to fix and not a judgment of the drawing or of Sarita.

grounding: Shows a child feeling the whole self judged after a correction, and a teacher separating the fix from the worth of the child.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage: Note from class teacher, Friday. During spelling correction today, Deepak received his notebook with "recieve" marked wrong. He pushed the book away and said the teacher's board was wrong. He crossed his arms and would not look up. I did not argue. I sat beside him and showed him the word in the dictionary, then asked him to find it himself. He did, quietly. Then I told him one wrong letter does not cancel the four he got right on that line. He wrote the word three times. He asked if he could keep the eraser. Please praise the four correct spellings at home before the fifth. Himani, class teacher

qa.q: Which word was marked wrong in Deepak's notebook?
qa.a: The word "recieve" was marked wrong in Deepak's notebook.

qa.q: What was Deepak feeling when he pushed the book away and crossed his arms?
qa.a: Deepak felt hurt and defensive, and his claim that the board was wrong shows the mistake stung him.

qa.q: What could Deepak's parents do at home to support him after this?
qa.a: They could first praise what he got right in his spelling and then look at the one wrong letter with him calmly, without turning it into a judgment of him.

qa.q: How does Himani see Deepak's reaction?
qa.a: Himani sees it as hurt more than defiance, which is why the teacher sat beside him, used a dictionary and pointed out the four correct letters.

grounding: Shows a child crumpling and arguing after correction, and a teacher patiently separating one mistake from the child's worth.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage: Noor was sitting behind Sarita in science on Wednesday when the teacher said the model volcano's label was hard to read and the crater too small. Sarita spun around in her chair. "The glue was old! Also Riya knocked it! Also nobody told us the size!" The teacher waited until she stopped, then moved on. Sarita sat with her arms folded until the bell. But at lunch, Noor saw her outside the lab with a marker, quietly rewriting the label in bigger letters. She widened the crater with her thumbs. Noor kept walking, and pretended not to have seen anything.

qa.q: What did the teacher say was wrong with the volcano model?
qa.a: The teacher said the label was hard to read and the crater was too small.

qa.q: What does Sarita's list of excuses suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt stung and proud, and wanted to defend herself before she could take in the feedback.

qa.q: What could Sarita try next time she gets feedback like this?
qa.a: She could listen to the whole comment and write it down before answering, then decide privately what to change.

qa.q: Why might Noor pretend not to have seen Sarita fixing the label?
qa.a: Noor seems to see that Sarita is quietly using the feedback and wants to spare her pride, so saying nothing lets her keep her dignity.

grounding: Shows a teenager listing excuses when critiqued but privately using the useful part later, with a classmate observing.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage:
Monday. Vidya ma'am handed back Dhruv's essay with a line under the first paragraph: "Too long. Start at your second sentence." Dhruv said the printer had jammed, exams were on, and the topic was too wide anyway. Vidya ma'am let him finish and said only, "Think about it."
Tuesday night. At his desk, Dhruv opened the file and looked at the first paragraph for a long minute. He deleted the opening sentence and began at the second.
The next Monday, Vidya ma'am read the new version and said, "This is much clearer." Dhruv shrugged. "I was going to change it anyway."

qa.q: What did Vidya ma'am write under the first paragraph of Dhruv's essay?
qa.a: She wrote "Too long. Start at your second sentence."

qa.q: What did Dhruv's remark "I was going to change it anyway" show he was feeling?
qa.a: It showed his pride, since he wanted to keep the feeling that the change was his own idea instead of admitting he had taken the advice.

qa.q: What turning point happened on Tuesday night?
qa.a: Dhruv opened the file alone, looked at the first paragraph and started at the second sentence, using the feedback once no one was watching.

qa.q: How might Vidya ma'am see Dhruv's excuses on Monday?
qa.a: She lets him finish and says only "Think about it," which suggests she sees the excuses as pride and trusts him to use the point later.

grounding: Shows a teenager defensive on the first day and quietly using the feedback in private on later days.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage:
Monday, Tanuja had a half-built cardboard model of her water-testing kit and an urge to hide it until it looked neat. Her mentor, Naveen sir, was free at four. She almost skipped it.
Tuesday, red-faced, she put the rough model on his desk. He turned it over and said, "Your sensor sits above the waterline. It will never touch the sample." She felt small and relieved at once.
Friday, she rebuilt the base with the sensor lower. It took an afternoon. She thought about the three weeks she would have spent building on the wrong plan.

qa.q: When did Tanuja put the rough model on the mentor's desk?
qa.a: She put the rough cardboard model on Naveen sir's desk on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she put the model on the desk?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed because the model was rough, but also relieved that the mistake was found early.

qa.q: What did Tanuja change after the feedback?
qa.a: She rebuilt the base with the sensor set lower, which took only an afternoon.

qa.q: How does Naveen sir see the rough model?
qa.a: Naveen sir treats it as something he can check quickly and correct at once, so an early look saves Tanuja from a long wrong build.

grounding: Shows a student sharing a rough model with a mentor early despite embarrassment and avoiding weeks of building the wrong thing.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
passage: I am Swati, and I want to tell you about my thesis year. I had planned three weeks to build a survey on how buses run late in my town. I was ashamed of my outline, one messy page, so I nearly waited till it was perfect. My guide, Sabina ma'am, had a free hour, so I took the page to her, blushing. She read it and said, "A report from two years ago already has this answer. Use their numbers, and ask what they missed." I sat in the corridor afterwards, half stunned. Three weeks saved. That mess of a page was the cheapest thing I ever showed anyone.

qa.q: How long had Swati planned to spend building the survey?
qa.a: Swati had planned three weeks to build the survey.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling as Swati took the outline to Sabina ma'am?
qa.a: Swati was blushing and ashamed of the messy page, but went anyway.

qa.q: What choice by Swati saved weeks of work?
qa.a: Taking the messy outline to Sabina ma'am early, instead of waiting until it was perfect.

qa.q: What did Sabina ma'am see in the outline that Swati had missed?
qa.a: Sabina ma'am knew a report from two years ago already had the answer, so she could point Swati to use those numbers and look for what was missing.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling showing a rough outline to a mentor early despite embarrassment and saving weeks of wasted building.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
subtype: Quick cycles of try, check, adjust [Response]
passage: I wanted a small automatic plant-waterer for my hostel window, so I did not start with the good design. Version one was a bottle, a straw and tape; I tested it with a cup of water and it leaked at the cap. I wrote "seal" in my notebook. Version two used clay at the cap and dripped too fast. "Slow it," I wrote. By version five, with a knotted thread as a wick, it dripped once every few seconds. My friend Himani laughed at the mountain of tape but watched it hold all evening. Each try cost me almost nothing. Madhav

qa.q: What did Madhav use as a wick in version five?
qa.a: Madhav used a knotted thread as a wick in version five.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling as the versions failed, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Madhav seems calm and curious, because a short note follows each failure and another try starts without giving up.

qa.q: Why did Madhav test with a cup of water instead of building the good design first?
qa.a: A small test costs almost nothing and shows exactly what is wrong, such as the leak or the too-fast drip, so each mistake becomes cheap information.

qa.q: How does Himani see Madhav's pile of tape?
qa.a: Himani laughs at the mountain of tape but is impressed enough to watch it hold all evening.

grounding: Shows a maker building a small version, testing, noting what is wrong and revising in quick cycles.

subtopic: Feedback loops and iteration
subtype: Quick cycles of try, check, adjust [Response]
passage: Note from workshop supervisor. Today Saurabh set out to make a phone stand and did not touch the plywood. He cut a stand from cardboard in ten minutes, put his phone on it and watched it tip backwards. He added a rear leg and tried again, then made the slot deeper when the phone slid. Four cardboard versions later, he took the measurements to the saw. I asked him why he had not cut wood first. He said, "Cardboard mistakes are free." The final stand held the phone through a full video call. Nothing was wasted but paper. Disha, workshop supervisor

qa.q: How long did it take Saurabh to cut the first cardboard stand?
qa.a: It took Saurabh ten minutes to cut the first stand from cardboard.

qa.q: What might Saurabh have been thinking when he watched the phone tip backwards?
qa.a: He was probably curious and unbothered, seeing the tip as information about the missing leg, since he simply added one and tried again.

qa.q: What would you advise a beginner who wants to skip the cardboard step?
qa.a: Try a cheap version first, check what fails, then change one thing, so mistakes cost paper instead of good wood.

qa.q: How does Disha view Saurabh's approach as a supervisor?
qa.a: Disha watches him and records that nothing was wasted but paper, which shows the supervisor sees short test loops as sensible.

grounding: Shows a maker building a small cheap version, testing it and revising several times before the costly version.
